title: Well-being
text:
What this section is
This section provides teachers with educational classroom routines that support student well-being. It is designed to support attention, reflection, self-regulation, classroom climate, mindfulness, and transitions.
It is not counselling, psychotherapy, diagnosis, treatment, or a replacement for school mental-health services.
Students should never be required to disclose private experiences, trauma, diagnoses, family circumstances, or personal mental-health information as part of these activities.
If a student needs individual support, teachers should follow school and board procedures and involve the appropriate school professionals and administrators.

title: Well-being
text:
Professional scope
The Ontario College of Teachers describes supporting students’ mental health as part of professional practice. Its guidance emphasizes supportive learning environments, recognizing concerns, helping students connect with appropriate supports, and maintaining professional boundaries.
The College also cautions teachers not to move into counselling unless counselling is part of their role and they have the appropriate training. Technology Commons uses that boundary here: these are short teaching routines, not therapy.
Teachers should continue to follow employer, school board, school, and Ministry policies.

Ontario College of Teachers: Professional Boundaries

title: Well-being
text:
Beginning every class
The opening routine should usually take about 3 to 5 minutes.

Quote on the board. A short quotation, question, proverb, observation, or idea connected to learning, effort, curiosity, craft, responsibility, attention, or community.
Well-being activity. A brief, approachable activity that helps the class settle and shift attention into the room.
Today’s intention. One sentence about what students are about to learn, make, investigate, repair, or improve.

The activity should feel like a classroom ritual rather than a clinical exercise.

title: Well-being
text:
Ending every class
The closing routine should also take about 3 to 5 minutes.

Pause and reset. Stop work, put tools or devices into a safe state, and clear the immediate workspace.
Reflect. Use one short prompt, observation, or playful attention activity.
Close the loop. Identify what was completed, what remains unfinished, and the first useful action for next class.

For shop classes, the closing routine also supports safe cleanup and a deliberate transition away from tools and equipment.

title: Well-being
text:
Activity ideas

Notice five
Without speaking, notice five things you can see, four sounds you can hear, three physical sensations, two colours you had not noticed before, and one thing you are ready to focus on.


One-minute build observation
Place an ordinary object, component, tool, fastener, or machine part where everyone can see it. Students silently notice as many design decisions as they can in one minute. Ask for observations about shape, material, joints, manufacturing, ergonomics, function, or failure points.


Comfortable-count breathing, optional
Invite students to breathe in, pause, breathe out, and pause for comfortable counts. Keep the activity optional. Do not present it as treatment for anxiety or another condition.


Sound map
For 30 to 60 seconds, students listen without talking and mentally map sounds as near, medium, or far away. Then return attention to the room.


Precision challenge
Ask students to estimate when 30 seconds has passed without checking a clock. Compare estimates and connect the result to measurement, calibration, tolerance, or human perception.


One good question
Give students 60 seconds to write one question they are curious about today. It can be technical, practical, or connected to the day’s work. No personal disclosure is required.


Reset the workspace
Students take one quiet minute to arrange only what they need for the next task. In a computer class this can mean closing distractions and opening the required files. In a shop it can mean checking PPE, tools, and work-area readiness.


Closing snapshot
Students answer one of these privately or aloud, depending on the class:

What changed in your understanding today?
What worked better than expected?
What failed in a useful way?
What is the first thing you should do next class?
What would you explain differently if teaching this to someone else?

title: NICE Design Process
text: Design does not start with a solution. It starts with a situation. NICE gives you four simple steps to understand the situation, make something, test it, and improve it.

title: NICE Design Process
text:
Start with the Situation
What is happening? Who is involved? Where will the design be used? What might change?
The situation is the frame around the whole design process. If the situation changes, your needs, research, design, and evaluation may need to change too.



The NICE design process inside a situation

A rounded rectangle labelled Situation contains four connected stages: Needs and Necessities, Inquire and Investigate, Create and Communicate, and Evaluate. The arrows form a loop.       SITUATION The context around the design can change.
   
 N Needs & Necessities
 I Inquire & Investigate
 C Create & Communicate
 E Evaluate
Learn, make, test, repeat.

title: NICE Design Process
text:
N: Needs & Necessities
Ask: What must the design do, and what would make it better?
A need is a clear requirement. It should usually be testable as yes or no.

Need: must weigh less than 10 kg.
Need: must fit inside a 500 mm space.

A necessity is something where more or less can be better. It can be scored or weighted.

Necessity: lighter is better.
Necessity: easier to use is better.
Necessity: more durable is better.

A necessity can become a need when the situation requires it. “Lightweight” is a preference until the situation says the object must weigh less than 10 kg.

title: NICE Design Process
text:
I: Inquire & Investigate
Ask: What do we need to learn before we decide what to make?
Look at users, existing products, materials, measurements, experiments, books, websites, videos, AI tools, and ideas from other fields.
For useful inquiry, record four things:

What did you investigate?
How did you investigate it?
What did you learn?
How could that change your design?

Good designers rarely start from nothing. They study what already exists, borrow useful ideas, combine technologies, and improve them for a new situation.

title: NICE Design Process
text:
C: Create & Communicate
Ask: What is the simplest thing we can make that lets us test and explain the idea?
That might be a sketch, cardboard model, CAD model, circuit, mock-up, code prototype, or working part.
Do not wait for a perfect final product. Make enough to learn something, show it to other people, and get useful feedback.

title: NICE Design Process
text:
E: Evaluate
Ask: Did it work, and are we still solving the right problem?
Test the design against the requirements you wrote earlier:

Does it meet every need? Pass or fail.
How well does it meet each necessity? Score and compare.
What did testing or feedback teach you?
Were the original needs and necessities correct?
Did the situation change?

Evaluation is not the end. What you learn sends you back around the NICE cycle.

title: NICE Design Process
section: A quick example: how phones changed
text:
A quick example: how phones changed
A landline telephone solved long-distance voice communication, but it kept the user attached to a wire. Radio communication allowed people to communicate while moving. Combining ideas from telephone networks and radio helped make mobile phones possible.
Then the situation kept changing. People wanted smaller phones, text messaging, email, cameras, maps, internet access, apps, and eventually communication that could move onto watches and other wearables.
The important idea is not that one person invented the modern phone. It is that designers kept investigating existing ideas, combining them, testing them, and responding to changing needs.

title: NICE Design Process
text:
Remember

The goal is not to get the first design right. The goal is to learn enough each cycle to make the next decision better.

title: N.I.C.E. Design
text:
Before teaching at Port Credit, I was walking through a park along the Mississauga lakeshore in January and wondering how I was going to teach technological design well. Mechatronics had made me comfortable with mechanical, electrical, controls, and robotics design. Wood, aesthetics, material expression, and craft were less familiar territory.
There is also a small joke built into the name. After enough iteration, testing, and user feedback, the response you hope to hear is: “Nice design.”
Looking at the trees, I started thinking about wood as a material with its own properties and history. More importantly, I started thinking about design as a natural cycle rather than a straight sequence.

title: N.I.C.E. Design
text:
Too many boxes
The design-process models I knew were useful, but they were difficult to hold in your head while actually building something. The older Ontario technological education process made iteration explicit. TeachEngineering uses Ask, Research, Imagine, Plan, Create, Test, Improve, then repeat. SPICE compresses the work into Situation, Problem, Ideas and Investigation, Choose and Construct, and Evaluation.





Older Ontario technological education design process.


Ontario design process source




TeachEngineering engineering design process.


TeachEngineering design process


Mr. Elsie’s technology education page also brings the Ontario process and SPICE together in one place. The SPICE model shown there was created by Mr. Franzen: SPICE Design Flow Chart.

title: N.I.C.E. Design
text:
N.I.C.E.
I wanted something simple enough to remember at a workbench:

N - Needs and Necessities
I - Investigate and Inquire
C - Create and Communicate
E - Evaluate

The important move is E back to N.
An MVP or prototype gives us something real to test. Evaluation asks whether the solution met the needs, but it should also ask whether we understood the needs correctly in the first place. Users may reveal priorities they could not describe before seeing or using a solution. The best inventions sometimes expose needs people did not yet know how to name.

title: N.I.C.E. Design
text:
A spiral, not a circle
I do not picture N.I.C.E. Design as a flat loop. I picture it rising as it repeats. At the bottom, the problem is broad and poorly defined. Each cycle adds evidence, user feedback, failures, and better questions. The spiral becomes tighter as it rises, like the shape of a coniferous tree.

N.I.C.E. SPIRAL DIAGRAM PLACEHOLDER
Show N -> I -> C -> E -> N climbing upward in repeated loops. The lower loops are broad and uncertain. The upper loops become tighter and better defined, forming the profile of a coniferous tree.

N.I.C.E. Design is not meant to remove the complexity of design. It is meant to give that complexity a four-letter structure students can remember while they are doing the work.

title: From a University Sketch to a Logo and Commons Emblem
section: A personal logo should stay simple
text:
A personal logo should stay simple
My original AA mark came from university. It was thin, angular, and easy to draw by hand.



The original AA mark I made while I was in university.


Years later, I changed it because I had changed. As I evolved as an educator and became more mature, I wanted the mark to feel less sharp and more supportive. I made the strokes heavier and curved the cross-arms.



The revised AA mark with heavier strokes and curved cross-arms.


The curve feels more supportive than a straight bar. It can suggest an arch, a truss, an umbrella, part of a circle, an arrow, or the leading edge of a kite. Those references matter to me, but the logo does not need to explain all of them to everyone who sees it.
That is the point of a personal logo. It should be simple, memorable, reproducible, and recognizable at a small size. It should represent you without trying to tell your entire life story.

title: From a University Sketch to a Logo and Commons Emblem
section: Identity can change without rejecting where it came from
text:
Identity can change without rejecting where it came from
I am a disciple of Jesus, and I worship one God in three persons: the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.
My own emphasis has changed over time. Earlier, I thought most about God as Creator. Later, I focused more on Jesus, the Son, who lived on earth and showed what faith could look like in a human life. More recently, I have tried to honour the Holy Spirit, whom I believe lives and works in each person. That has pushed me to think more about dignity, relationship, service, community, and how I treat the people around me.
My Christian faith is my own foundation, but I also want to keep learning about the religions, philosophies, and spiritual traditions represented by the people around me. As an educator, I want to understand students better, including the beliefs, practices, stories, and values that may be important to them. That means listening with respect rather than assuming that everyone sees meaning, community, duty, suffering, nature, or the sacred in the same way I do.
I find wisdom worth studying in many ancient traditions. Indigenous teachings about responsibility to future generations, including the Seven Generations principle, challenge me to think beyond the immediate moment. Taoism’s attention to balance, humility, and living in relationship with the natural world resonates with me. Buddhism raises powerful questions about compassion, attachment, suffering, and attention. Judaism carries a deep tradition of study, questioning, covenant, memory, and responsibility. Sikhism emphasizes service, equality, courage, and community. Islam offers rich traditions of prayer, charity, discipline, mercy, and submission to God. Hindu traditions contain diverse teachings about duty, knowledge, devotion, action, and the nature of reality. I also want to learn from Jainism, the Bahá’í Faith, humanist traditions, and other ways people have tried to understand how to live well with one another.
I do not see these traditions as interchangeable, and learning about them does not require me to give up my own beliefs. It helps me approach other people with more curiosity and less certainty about what their experience must be. In a classroom, that matters. Students should be able to bring different identities and beliefs into the same shared space while still working, learning, building, questioning, and treating one another with dignity.
Those beliefs and influences are part of who I am, but a public educational identity does not need to explain all of them literally. Instead, some of those ideas can appear more indirectly through forms that suggest guidance, support, light, growth, roots, water, connection, and place.

title: From a University Sketch to a Logo and Commons Emblem
section: From a personal logo to a Commons emblem
text:
From a personal logo to a Commons emblem
The larger symbol is doing a different job. It represents Technology Commons, not just me, so it can carry more information than the AA logo.
The current emblem combines several ideas:

the AA structure represents my authorship and support for the Commons
the lighthouse connects to Port Credit Secondary School and suggests guidance and stewardship
the rocket-like upward form connects the identity to science, technology, engineering, and aspiration
the water connects to Port Credit, flow, movement, and learning
the roots suggest heritage, growth, and a foundation that can exist even below the visible waterline
the enclosing circle makes the image read as a shared organizational emblem rather than only a personal monogram

The lighthouse, leaves, roots, waves, and light did not arrive at once. Early versions added too much. Other versions became so simple that they lost the character I wanted. The current version sits between those extremes.

title: From a University Sketch to a Logo and Commons Emblem
text:
The final lighthouse system
The selected emblem also has to work as a system, not only as one full-colour image. It needs transparent and white-background versions, monochrome versions for limited-colour use, a reversed version for dark surfaces, and small-size exports for icons and favicons.



This is the end point of the emblem work for now. The images above should show how the design got here without pretending every experiment was equally important.
For students, that is the part worth copying. Start with a mark you can draw. Make several versions. Keep the rejected ideas. Test everything in black and white and at small size. Then decide whether you are making a personal logo, which should remain compact, or an emblem for an organization, product, project, or community, which may have room to carry a larger story.
The first sketch and the final emblem matter. Most of the design happened between them.

title: About Technology Commons
text:
Technology Commons is an open teaching project for learning technology by designing, building, testing, explaining, and improving real work.
The idea is simple:

Come with a question. Leave with something you understand well enough to use, test, build, or explain.

The site brings lessons, projects, tools, references, classroom routines, and research into one shared place for technology education.


Technology courses move constantly between thinking and doing. A student may need to understand a measurement, make a sketch, write code, diagnose a fault, choose a material, use a machine, test an idea, and explain what happened, sometimes all in the same project.
Technology Commons is designed around the kinds of questions that appear while doing that work:

> How do I turn an idea into something that actually works?
> How precise does this measurement need to be, and which tool should I use?
> Why did this prototype, program, circuit, or repair fail, and what should I change next?
> How can I show the decisions, evidence, and learning behind the finished result?
// goal: learn by making, testing, explaining, and improving

The aim is not to separate theory from practice. It is to build clear mental models through real work, then use evidence from that work to improve the next attempt.



ROLE: CLASSROOM :: WORKSHOP :: COMMONS

Technology Commons supports three secondary technology course groups: TAS2O Exploring Technologies, TEJ3M / TEJ4M Computer Engineering Technology, and TTJ3C / TTJ4C Transportation Technology.
Each course has its own pathway, but they share common ideas: safe work, measurement, design, technical communication, iteration, evidence, reflection, and the responsibility to leave useful knowledge behind for others.
The word commons is intentional. Useful knowledge should be shared, inspected, improved, and reused. Students should be able to find what they need today, while educators should be able to inspect the structure and adapt what is useful elsewhere.


Projects use the NICE cycle:

title: About Technology Commons
text:
Technology courses move constantly between thinking and doing. A student may need to understand a measurement, make a sketch, write code, diagnose a fault, choose a material, use a machine, test an idea, and explain what happened, sometimes all in the same project.
Technology Commons is designed around the kinds of questions that appear while doing that work:

> How do I turn an idea into something that actually works?
> How precise does this measurement need to be, and which tool should I use?
> Why did this prototype, program, circuit, or repair fail, and what should I change next?
> How can I show the decisions, evidence, and learning behind the finished result?
// goal: learn by making, testing, explaining, and improving

The aim is not to separate theory from practice. It is to build clear mental models through real work, then use evidence from that work to improve the next attempt.

10 in the Zone



Also called: 10 Checkers in the Zone, Ten in the Zone


Ten in the Zone means having ten checkers in your home board and outer board, giving you strong attacking or blitzing potential.



The zone is your side of the board, consisting of your home board and outer board. At the start of the game, you have eight checkers in the attacking zone. Bringing two active builders down from the mid-point increases that number to ten.


With ten checkers in the zone, you have strong blitzing potential. Nine checkers is borderline, while eight or fewer generally makes a blitz less effective.

25 Percent Rule



Also called: 25% Rule


The 25 Percent Rule says that, if you ignore future recubes, you need about a 25 percent chance to take a double.



The 25 Percent Rule is a simplified baseline for cube decisions. In a holding game or other positions, if future cube actions are ignored, you need roughly a 25 percent winning chance to take a double. If the cube remains live and you may be able to recube later, you might correctly take with less than 25 percent.

8-9-12 Doubling Rule



Also called: 8-9-12 Rule


The 8-9-12 Doubling Rule is a guideline for doubling decisions in a pure race based on pip-count percentages.



In a pure race, the 8-9-12 Doubling Rule helps guide cube decisions. The percentage is calculated by dividing the difference between the two pip counts by the leader's pip count. The leader considers doubling at about 8 percent, the middle of the doubling window is around 9 percent, and the trailer can usually take when behind by up to about 12 percent.


For example, if the leader has a pip count of 60 and the trailer has 66, the difference is 6 pips. Six divided by 60 is 10 percent, placing the position within the doubling window.

ABT stands for the American Backgammon Tour, a series of major backgammon tournaments in the United States.

Ace-Point Game



An ace-point game is a holding game in which you hold an anchor on your opponent's one-point.



An ace-point game is a holding game in which you hold an anchor on your opponent's one-point. While your opponent bears in, you have about a 50 percent chance of getting a shot.


It is stronger than a two-point or three-point holding game because those anchors give you fewer opportunities to get a shot. The ace-point anchor therefore offers more hitting chances while the opponent brings their checkers home.

An acting captain is a chouette player who temporarily takes over the checker play when the original captain's game against the box ends but another cube remains active.



In a chouette, every team member controls their own cube. The captain makes the checker plays against the box.


For example, the captain may offer a double that the box passes. If the box still holds another player's cube, that player becomes the acting captain and continues the game against the box. The acting captain takes over the checker decisions for the remaining active game.

Adjusted Pip Count



An adjusted pip count modifies a pip count to account for checker distribution and bear-off efficiency.



An adjusted pip count is a pip count modified to account for checker distribution and bear-off efficiency. Large gaps and tall stacks usually raise the adjusted pip count because they make a position less efficient. Adjusted pip counts are commonly used to judge who is really ahead in a race, especially when making cube decisions. Methods include Keith Count, Trice Count, and the iSight method.

Advanced Anchor



An advanced anchor is an anchor on your opponent's four-point or five-point.



An advanced anchor is an anchor on your opponent's four-point or five-point. It gives you outfield control and helps your back checkers escape. It is particularly useful in holding games, and you generally try not to break it until late in the middlegame or endgame.

Ahead in the Count



Also called: Ahead in the Race


Ahead in the Count means having a lower pip count than your opponent and therefore being ahead in the race.



Ahead in the Count means you have a lower pip count than your opponent, meaning you have fewer pips remaining to bring your checkers home and bear them off.


A common principle is, "When you are ahead in the race, race." Avoid unnecessary risk and contact, and focus on bringing your checkers home safely.

Ammunition describes checkers positioned where they can attack blots or build points.

An analog clock is a backgammon timing device with physical dials rather than digital displays.



An analog clock is a physical timing device with traditional dials and hands rather than digital displays. It tracks each player's remaining time during a backgammon match and helps ensure that the match is completed within the established time limits.

Anchor Game



An anchor game is a strategic game plan in which you hold one or more anchors in your opponent's home board, often while waiting for a shot that could turn the game around.



An anchor game is a strategic approach in which you retain one or more anchors, or made points, in your opponent's home board. These anchors give your checkers safety and allow you to wait for an opportunity to hit an exposed opposing checker. Anchor games are strongest when you also have a strong home board, making any successful hit more dangerous for your opponent.

Annotated Match



An annotated match is a recorded backgammon match whose rolls and plays have been entered into analysis software so the players' decisions can be reviewed.



An annotated match is usually video recorded, with each dice roll and checker play entered into an analysis engine such as eXtreme Gammon during or after the match. The engine analyzes the decisions, identifies mistakes, and calculates measures such as Performance Rating, or PR.


An annotated match may also include written or spoken commentary. BMAB uses analyzed match results when assessing player classifications. In formats such as UBC, players can also earn a point by recording a lower PR than their opponent.

Annotation



Annotation is the process of adding analysis to a backgammon match record.



Annotation is the process of entering each dice roll and checker play from a backgammon match into an analysis engine such as eXtreme Gammon. This is usually done from a video recording, either during the match or afterward.


The engine analyzes the players' decisions move by move and calculates measures such as PR. The resulting analysis can be used to study mistakes, assess playing strength, support BMAB classifications, or determine performance-based results in formats such as UBC.

Anti-Joker



An anti-joker is an extremely unlucky roll that usually leaves your position worse after the roll than it was before.



An anti-joker is an exceptionally unlucky roll, or sequence of rolls, that significantly worsens your position. Your position does not need to have been good beforehand; an anti-joker can make an already difficult position even worse. Because the result can feel especially harsh or unexpected, an anti-joker may contribute to tilt.

Army



Your army is your full group of checkers, viewed as a coordinated unit that should work together.



In backgammon, your army refers to all of your checkers. The term emphasizes that your checkers should work together as a coordinated unit rather than acting as isolated pieces.


A strong army has good formation, connected checkers, and continuity across the board. This allows the checkers to support one another, create useful points, and carry out a common game plan.



Categories: Game Plans & Position Types, Slang & Expressions





Around the Corner



Around the Corner means moving a checker from your opponent's outer board into your own outer board.



Around the Corner describes the transition in which a checker moves from your opponent's outer board, past the mid-point, and into your own outer board. This brings the checker onto your side of the board and closer to your home board.


The move often marks progress from the early game toward bringing your checkers home and eventually bearing them in.

Asset



An asset is a useful positional feature that works in your favour and improves your winning chances.



In backgammon, an asset is any useful feature of your position that increases your winning chances. Assets can include a made point, a strong anchor, a strong prime, a strong home board, or an advantageous checker distribution.


You consider your assets when making checker-play and cube decisions, including whether your position is strong enough to double or whether you have enough positional resources to take an opponent's cube.



Category: Game Plans & Position Types





Attack



An attack is an aggressive play intended to hit or threaten opposing blots and improve your position.



An attack is a deliberate play aimed at hitting one or more of your opponent's blots, often to gain a positional or timing advantage. Blitzing and trying to close out your opponent are common forms of attack.


Attacking can also help your back checkers escape. When you have several checkers trapped behind your opponent, hitting can put an opposing checker on the bar instead of leaving your own checkers vulnerable to being put on the bar.



Category: Checker Play



See also



Attack Zone


Attacking Game







Attack Zone



Also called: The Zone, Your Side of the Board, Zone, Zone of Attack


The attack zone is your side of the board, consisting of your home board and outer board.



The attack zone is your side of the board: your home board and outer board. It is the area where you can use your ammunition to attack opposing checkers, launch a blitz, make home-board points, or try to close out your opponent.

Attacking Game



An attacking game is a game plan based on hitting, closing points, and keeping opposing checkers on the bar.



An attacking game is a game plan based on hitting, closing points, and keeping opposing checkers on the bar. The most famous type of attacking game is a blitz, where in the early to middle game you repeatedly attack your opponent, put their checkers on the bar, and try to close them out.



Category: Game Plans & Position Types

Attack

Automatic Doubles



Also called: Automatic, Automatic Double, Automatics


Automatic Doubles is an optional money-game rule where matching opening rolls automatically double the game's value.



Automatic Doubles is an optional rule used in money play. If both players roll the same number while determining who moves first, the game's value automatically doubles. The doubling cube is turned to 2 but remains centered, so neither player owns it and either player may offer the next double. Players normally agree before playing whether to use this rule and may limit the number of automatic doubles allowed in one game.



Categories: Cube Action, Rules & Procedures, Chouette & Money Play





Awkward Number



An awkward number is a roll that leaves no clearly good checker play, forcing you to choose among several suboptimal options.



An awkward number is a roll that creates a difficult checker-play decision because none of the available moves fits the position well. The challenge is not choosing between two strong plays, but identifying the least damaging option among several suboptimal ones.


An awkward number is related to an anti-joker, but the emphasis is different. An anti-joker describes an exceptionally bad roll that worsens your position, while an awkward number describes the difficulty of the decision because there is no obvious checker play.



Categories: Checker Play, Slang & Expressions



See also



Awkward Position


Anti-Joker







Awkward Position



An awkward position is a position in which many rolls leave no clearly constructive checker play.



An awkward position has poor flexibility, distribution, connectivity, or checker coordination, causing many rolls to produce difficult choices among suboptimal plays. The player often has no obvious constructive move and must choose the option that does the least damage.


An awkward position is different from an awkward number. The position is the underlying board structure that makes many rolls difficult, while an awkward number is one particular roll that creates a difficult decision.



Categories: Checker Play, Game Plans & Position Types

Back Game



Also called: Backgame


A back game is a strategy based on holding two or more points deep in your opponent's home board while waiting for a late opportunity to hit.



A back game is a highly technical and volatile game plan in which you hold two or more points deep in your opponent's home board. Good timing is essential. If you are forced to break your board or kill checkers, the back game loses much of its effectiveness. It is common to be 70 to 100 pips behind in the race and still have meaningful winning chances.


Back-game play can be counterintuitive. Sometimes you avoid hitting because the hit would give your opponent additional timing, while being hit may help recycle one of your checkers and maintain your own timing. Back games can involve substantial cube action and high cube values. They occur relatively infrequently, generally in fewer than 10 percent of games, so beginners should study more common game plans first. Understanding back games becomes increasingly important when progressing from expert play toward master level and beyond.



Category: Game Plans & Position Types





BMAB



Also called: Backgammon Masters Awarding Body


BMAB stands for the Backgammon Masters Awarding Body, an organization that awards backgammon titles based on verified performance ratings.



The Backgammon Masters Awarding Body, commonly called BMAB, awards mastership titles and proficiency certificates using Performance Rating from verified, analyzed matches. Players must complete the required amount of qualifying play and meet the applicable PR standard.

Fischer Increment



Also called: Bonus Time, Fischer Time, Increment


Fischer Increment adds a fixed amount of time to a player's bank for each turn, allowing unused time to accumulate.



Fischer Increment credits a fixed amount of time for each turn. Depending on the clock or software, the increment may be credited at the start of the turn or after the completed turn. Unlike Simple Delay, the full increment is cumulative. If a player uses less time than the increment, their time bank grows.



Categories: Board, Equipment & Notation, Rules & Procedures

P1 terms




Performance Rating



Also called: ER, Error Rate, Performance Rate, PR


Performance Rating, or PR, measures how closely your checker plays and cube decisions match the moves chosen to be "correct" by an analysis bot.



Performance Rating, usually shortened to PR and sometimes called Error Rate or ER, is a number used to judge how well you played an analyzed match. A PR of 0 means the bot found no mistakes in your checker plays or cube decisions. As a rough guide, newer players may play around 20 to 40 PR, intermediate players around 10 to 20, and advanced players below 10. Different bots can produce different ratings, so results from different programs should not be compared directly.


When describing your PR across several matches, combine the value lost across all counted decisions and divide by the total number of those decisions. Do not take a simple average of the separate match PRs, because matches can contain very different numbers of decisions. Lower-PR, more skilled players win more often over large samples, although the PR from one match can be affected by Winner's Curse.

Reserve Time



Also called: Bank Time, Clock Reserve Time, Time Bank


Reserve time is the bank of clock time a player can use across a match after any per-move delay has expired.



Reserve time is the main bank of time available to a player across an entire match or playing session. With Simple Delay, the delay is used first on each turn, and reserve time begins to count down only after the delay expires.


Under Fischer Increment, a fixed amount of time is credited to this bank for each turn, so the bank can increase when moves are played quickly.

Also called: Delay Time, Time Delay, US Delay


Simple Delay gives a player a fixed amount of use-it-or-lose-it time at the start of every turn before reserve time begins to count down.



Simple Delay provides a fixed amount of time at the start of each turn. The delay counts down before the player's reserve time begins to decrease. If the turn is completed within the delay, no reserve time is used. Any unused delay disappears and does not carry forward.

UBC



Also called: Ultimate Backgammon Championship


UBC stands for the Ultimate Backgammon Championship, a competition in which match results and Performance Rating both contribute to the standings.



The Ultimate Backgammon Championship, commonly called UBC, rewards both winning matches and playing with a lower Performance Rating. A match can award one point for the match win and a separate point for the PR win, allowing a player to earn zero, one, or two points.

Winner's Curse



Winner's Curse is the tendency for favourable rolls that help a player win to also create more difficult decisions, making the winner's match PR look worse than usual.



Winners often roll more doubles and other strong rolls, hit more checkers, and put their opponent on the bar more often. These favourable rolls improve their chances of winning, but they can also create more decisions and several good-looking moves, making it harder to choose the very best play. A winning position can also make it easier to miss a double or send the cube too late.


Winner's Curse does not mean winners are usually less skilled or play with a higher PR. Lower-PR, more skilled players still win more often, especially over longer matches or sessions. It means that the same favourable rolls that help produce a win can also make that winning path unusually difficult to play accurately.



Category: Analysis & Probability

title: Reviving the Blog: Lessons From a Bugle, a Flag, and a Forgotten Story
text:
FROM THE ARCHIVE
Originally published on andrewandrade.ca. This version is included in Lore because it captures the kind of learning record this section is meant to preserve: teaching, history, identity, community, and the things carried forward.
View the source history on GitHub
It’s been years since I last wrote here. I started this blog back in fourth-year engineering while job hunting, before I joined Palantir, before robotics labs and late-night debugging sessions, before teaching, before all the twists that came after.
This week, Remembrance Day brought me back.
I had the honour of playing trumpet with our school band, not the Last Post; I’m still working to be good enough for that, but enough to stand with the group in something meaningful. Instruments in hand, everything paused for a moment, and it pulled me right back to my time in army cadets.
Even now, that first year is burned into my memory: awkward uniform, barely any badges, trying to figure out what leadership meant. Luckily we had mentors to guide us.
Cadets taught me that rank wasn’t the patch; it was the work behind it.
As we approached Remembrance Day this year, I found myself thinking about the small rituals that shaped me. Raising the flag was one of them.
Sometimes it was early, cold, or rushed, but it mattered. And I wasn’t alone.
Music also became part of those mornings, including our national anthem.
Fast-forward to high school robotics, coding, and engineering, different worlds entirely, but the same threads of discipline and responsibility ran through them.
I didn’t stay long enough in cadets to stack up badges like the mentors I admired, but the two years I spent there were full. Varied, intense, and formative, but I still loved computers.
This year, as part of preparing for our ceremony, I learned more than I expected, thanks entirely to the Student Activity Council, who did all the research.
That’s where I discovered the story of George Cardozo, one of the “Port Credit Boys.”

title: Reviving the Blog: Lessons From a Bugle, a Flag, and a Forgotten Story
section: The Bugler They Didn’t Let Become an Officer
text:
The Bugler They Didn’t Let Become an Officer
George’s story starts decades before mine, but strangely close to home.
He was a Jamaican-born teacher, educated in Port-au-Prince and Kingston, who came to Canada and enlisted with the 4th Battalion, Canadian Expeditionary Force, on 22 September 1914.
One of the first recruits at Valcartier.



George standing


His attestation paper recorded only the essentials: his trade or calling, his date of birth, and his place of birth. Beyond those brief entries, the rest of George’s life, identity, and service must be reconstructed through the surviving evidence gathered from archival and family research.
A fuller picture, his experiences as a Jamaican-born bugler, his movement through the Canadian Expeditionary Force, and the context surrounding his enlistment, comes from the sources compiled in the project’s research. These include My Jamaican Family’s biography They Shall Grow Not Old: George Cardozo, a Casualty of …, the Canadian Virtual War Memorial entry for George Cordozo from Veterans Affairs Canada, and his digitized service file in Library and Archives Canada’s Personnel Records of the First World War.
Together, these sources allow us to understand George far more deeply than the minimal information captured on the photo.



George’s attestation paper


According to Dorothy Kew from the My Jamaican Family Blog, he was:

Five foot five
Dark complexion
“Coloured”
Roman Catholic
Teacher

With his education and background, he should have been an officer.
But because of his colour, he wasn’t given that chance.
Instead, they made him a bugler.



George sitting


Today, the role is ceremonial.
Back then, buglers woke before everyone else, played Reveille in the cold, roused officers, and handled the morning chores no one else wanted.
George still trained hard, at Ravina Barracks, on the SS Tyrolia to England, and finally to the Western Front.



Port Credit Boys


He died sometime between April 22 and 26, 1915, during the Second Battle of Ypres, the first time poison gas was used in the Great War. His body was never found.
His name is carved on the Menin Gate Memorial in Belgium with over 55,000 others who have no known grave.



Memorial


Every evening at 8 p.m., beneath his name, they still sound the Last Post.

title: Reviving the Blog: Lessons From a Bugle, a Flag, and a Forgotten Story
section: Bugles, Flags, and the Things We Carry Forward
text:
Bugles, Flags, and the Things We Carry Forward
This year I raised my trumpet high,
Not for the Last Post’s mournful cry,
But with a deeper, steadier sight
Of all the threads that shaped my flight.
I thought of flags I used to raise,
The badges missed in younger days,
The mentors’ paths I didn’t tread,
And those who served and marched instead.
I thought of George, so much like me,
A teacher-learner meant to be,
Who left to fight through smoke and flame
And never made it home again.

title: Reviving the Blog: Lessons From a Bugle, a Flag, and a Forgotten Story
text:
We Remember

“They shall grow not old, as we that are left grow old…”
- For the Fallen, Lawrence Binyon

This post is both a return and a reminder, of the past we inherit, the stories we uncover, and the unexpected ways they shape our present.
This Remembrance Day, I played the trumpet for our school.
But I also played it for George.
And I’m honoured to remember him here.

title: How Did the Phone Become This?
text:
Start here
A modern phone
Calls. Messages. Camera. Maps. Music. Games. Internet. Payment. School. Work.
How did one object end up doing all of this?

title: How Did the Phone Become This?
text:
Rewind
Before the smartphone, before the mobile phone, before the telephone:
People still needed to communicate.
The situation was different. The need was the same.

title: How Did the Phone Become This?
text:
Before electronics
People used visible or audible signals across distance:
fire and smoke
flags and semaphore
bells, horns, and drums
A signal could travel farther than a voice, but the message was limited.

title: How Did the Phone Become This?
text:
A string and two cups
A cup-and-string phone is not the ancestor of the cellphone.
It is a simple model of the problem:
How can sound move from one person to another?
Sound vibrates the cup. The string carries the vibration. The second cup turns it back into sound.
Useful idea, serious limitation: you are still connected by a line.

title: How Did the Phone Become This?
text:
Telegraph
Electricity made it possible to send a signal quickly through a wire.
New capability: long-distance messages could arrive much faster.
Limitation: the signal had to be encoded and decoded.
Design changed because the available technology changed.

title: How Did the Phone Become This?
text:
Telephone
The telephone changed the question:
What if the wire could carry a voice?
People could speak naturally over long distances.
But the phone was tied to a place.

title: How Did the Phone Become This?
text:
Radio
Radio changed another part of the situation:
What if communication did not need a wire?
Radio allowed communication while moving and where wires were impractical.
The trade-offs included equipment size, power, range, interference, and cost.

title: How Did the Phone Become This?
text:
Field radio
Military, emergency, aviation, marine, and industrial communication pushed radio toward portable systems.
Some early portable systems were backpack-sized.
They proved something important:
Wireless voice communication could move with the user.
But portable did not yet mean pocket-sized.

title: How Did the Phone Become This?
text:
Inquiry means looking sideways
A designer does not only ask, “What exists in phones?”
They also ask:

What does radio already do well?
What does the telephone network already do well?
What has the military learned about portable communication?
What can batteries and electronics now make possible?

Innovation often comes from combining existing ideas.

title: How Did the Phone Become This?
text:
Telephone + radio
Telephone networks were good at connecting one person to another.
Radio was good at communication without a fixed wire.
What happens when those ideas come together?
Mobile telephone

title: How Did the Phone Become This?
text:
The brick phone
The first useful mobile phones solved the biggest need:
Make a call while away from a landline.
But evaluation found obvious problems:

large
heavy
expensive
limited battery life

So the NICE cycle continued.

title: How Did the Phone Become This?
text:
The pocket phone
The question changed from:
Can a telephone be mobile?
To:
Can I comfortably carry it everywhere?
Nokia-era phones became smaller, tougher, simpler, and better at lasting through the day.

title: How Did the Phone Become This?
text:
Then people started typing
Voice was no longer enough.
Text messages and email changed what people wanted from a phone.
New need: enter information quickly.
BlackBerry-style devices used a full physical keyboard because typing had become important.

title: How Did the Phone Become This?
text:
The keyboard solved a problem
A physical keyboard made typing easier.
But it also created a new limitation:
The keyboard always takes up space.
Even when you are looking at a photo, map, video, game, or webpage.
Evaluation creates the next design question.

title: How Did the Phone Become This?
text:
Touchscreen
A touchscreen lets the same surface change jobs.
It can become:
keyboard | map | camera controls | game controls | browser | video
The phone is no longer only a telephone.
It becomes a small general-purpose computer.

title: How Did the Phone Become This?
text:
Apps change the situation again
Instead of deciding every future function when the phone is built, software can add new functions later.
The user may discover needs they could not have asked for before the technology existed.
Good design can reveal a need, not only respond to one.

title: How Did the Phone Become This?
text:
Consolidation
One device begins replacing many separate objects:
phone
camera
music player
GPS
calculator
calendar
flashlight
web browser
The design becomes a platform.

title: How Did the Phone Become This?
section: And then it spreads out again
text:
And then it spreads out again
Today, some phone functions move onto other devices:
smartwatch
earbuds
car displays
wearable sensors
The situation changes again: sometimes the best screen is the one you do not need to take out of your pocket.

title: How Did the Phone Become This?
section: The phone was never one invention
text:
The phone was never one invention
It was many cycles of:
Situation
N -> I -> C -> E
Changing needs. New research. New materials. New technologies. New prototypes. New feedback.
Then another cycle.

title: How Did the Phone Become This?
text:
NICE
N: Needs & Necessities
What must it do? What would make it better?
I: Inquire & Investigate
What can we learn from users, existing designs, experiments, and other fields?
C: Create & Communicate
What is the smallest useful version we can make and show?
E: Evaluate
Did it work? Are the requirements still right? Did the situation change?

title: How Did the Phone Become This?
text:
Design is a loop
Situation -> N -> I -> C -> E -> repeat
The goal is not to predict the perfect final product.
The goal is to make the next decision better than the last one.
